newsitem.title: GREECE: Greece braces for shortages from farmers blockade.
newsitem.headline: Greece braces for shortages from farmers blockade.

text.p: Greece braced for shortages as defiant farmers put up more barricades and vowed to continue their 11-day-old blockade that has crippled road and rail links.
With no sign of backing down from either the farmers or the socialist government, commercial and industrial unions warned of increasing damage to Greece's struggling economy.
"The Greek economy cannot be held hostage by some groups," nine Athens and Salonika unions said in a joint statement. "There are serious effects from the blockade of the national network."
Industries complained they are running short of fuel and merchants warned they may not be able to pay Christmas salaries if the blockade continues.
The food markets of Athens, the northern Greek city of Salonika and the central city of Larissa have started to feel the first pinch of shortages.
"I couldn't find any eggplant at the central market and the grocers said it was because of the blockade," said pensioner Maria Kyriakidou, 80.
Early estimates of the overall damage to the economy were conflicting but Athens newspapers said there was a loss of at least $12 million in just the first week of the protest.
The government has been adamant about not giving in to farmers' demands -- price supports, cheaper fuel, the rescheduling of $1.3 billion in debts and lower Value Added Tax on farming equipment.

Prime Minister Costas Simitis, facing his first big test since winning elections in September, has appealed to the farmers to understand Greece's obligations towards the European Union and give up their protest.

But he elicited little sympathy. On Saturday the farmers met and decided to boost and extend about 90 road and rail blocks. Farmers on the island of Crete said they would join in on Monday by barricading the road between the towns of Chania and Iraklio.

At makeshift campsites along the highways, where thousands of international trucks are trapped, farmers have decorated Christmas trees with their produce to indicate they were determined to stay through the holidays.

"The prime minister must review his stance because, as he can see, the road blocks are multiplying," said farmers' representative Yannis Patakis. "We are determined to continue. This is a struggle for survival."

With boisterous protest marches an almost daily event in Athens, Simitis fears bowing to the farmers could snowball, encouraging other groups to make demands on a 1997 austerity budget intended to set the economy on an EU convergence course.

"The price of satisfying the farmers' demands is $4 billion, equal to the amount which we are desperately trying to secure from new taxes and spending cuts in the budget," he told parliament on Friday.

Pensioners, high school teachers, hospital staff and doctors and construction workers have planned strikes and protest rallies this week, while the huge, powerful union of civil servants has called for a nationwide strike on December 17.
